stem: A Sickle cell disease patient who underwent bone marrow transplant. He got a fever 1 day after the procedure. He was started on ceftazidime but did not improve after 72 hours. There was no pneumonia or hypotension. What to add ?
why_right: Persistent fever on ceftazidime in a post-BMT neutropenic patient with no pneumonia, no hypotension (and, in the sister variant, no line or skin/mucosal lesions) means none of the indications for vancomycin are present. Fever that persists despite broad antibiotics in profound neutropenia raises invasive fungal infection, so an antifungal such as voriconazole (mould-active, first line for aspergillosis) is the keyed addition.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ceftriaxone lacks anti-pseudomonal cover, so adding or switching to it adds nothing to ceftazidime in neutropenia.
C. Sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) is used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis or treatment, not for unexplained persistent neutropenic fever.
D. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications (pneumonia, hypotension/sepsis, central line or skin infection, MRSA); the stem deliberately excludes these.
key_concept:
Persistent neutropenic fever: decide by the indication.
  • Pneumonia, shock, line or skin infection, MRSA: add vancomycin
  • None of these + fever persisting on antibiotics: add antifungal
  • Mould cover / aspergillosis: voriconazole
  • Empirical alternatives: echinocandin (caspofungin) or liposomal amphotericin
exam_pearl: Same BMT stem flips: WITH pneumonia = vancomycin, explicitly WITHOUT pneumonia/hypotension = antifungal.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient underwent BMT due to SCD, febrile neutropenia, given Ceftazidime, no improvement after 72 hours (No Pneumonia, No Hypotension, No Central Line, No Skin/Mucus Ulcerations)' with options Vancomycin / Tazocin / Ceftriaxone / Voriconazole; Voriconazole highlighted.

stem: patient with acute leukemia recently underwent allogenic bone marrow transplantation. After 2 weeks, she was neutropenic and developed a fever and cough. She was diagnosed with invasive aspergillosis based on radiological and microbiological assessment. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: A neutropenic patient early after allogeneic bone marrow transplantation is at high risk of invasive mould infection, and here invasive aspergillosis is already confirmed. Aspergillus is a fungus, and voriconazole is the first line treatment for invasive aspergillosis; it is also the only antifungal among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rifampicin: an antimycobacterial antibiotic used in TB and brucellosis; it has no antifungal activity.
B. Valaciclovir: an antiviral for herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections; no activity against Aspergillus.
C. Tigecycline: a broad spectrum antibacterial (glycylcycline) for resistant bacteria; it does not treat fungal infection.
key_concept:
Match the drug class to the organism.
  • Invasive aspergillosis: voriconazole first line
  • Mucormycosis: amphotericin B
  • Herpes viruses: aciclovir or valaciclovir
  • Mycobacteria: rifampicin based regimens
  • Risk factors for invasive mould: prolonged neutropenia, stem cell transplant, high dose steroids
exam_pearl: Do not confuse aspergillosis with mucormycosis: voriconazole covers Aspergillus but not Mucor, which needs amphotericin B.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Shown as a 'Q:' variant within block 776.

stem: Patient underwent bone marrow transplantation due to SCD, developed febrile neutropenia and has [NO] Pneumonia , she was given Ceftazidime and shows no improvement, what to add?
why_right: This recall's key is vancomycin: a post-BMT neutropenic patient on ceftazidime who is not improving. Ceftazidime has weak gram-positive activity (viridans streptococci from mucositis, staphylococci from lines), and vancomycin is the only option that adds gram-positive and MRSA cover; no antifungal is offered here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Tazocin is an alternative first-line anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam; it does not add meaningful new cover over ceftazidime for a non-responder.
C. Ceftriaxone has no anti-pseudomonal activity, so it is a downgrade in a neutropenic patient.
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is for Pneumocystis prophylaxis or treatment, not empirical escalation for neutropenic fever.
key_concept:
Escalation in febrile neutropenia:
  • Base: anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam
  • Vancomycin: pneumonia, sepsis/hypotension, line or skin infection, mucositis, MRSA
  • Antifungal: fever persisting after about 4 to 7 days
  • If the options include an antifungal and the stem excludes vancomycin triggers, pick the antifungal
exam_pearl: Check the options: if an antifungal is listed and pneumonia/hypotension/line infection are explicitly absent, the sister variant keys voriconazole.

stem: Ascitis treated by sparonolactone with no improvment , managment ?
key_concept:
Cirrhotic ascites ladder.
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Therapeutic paracentesis.
  • 1: treat cause, sodium restriction
  • 2: spironolactone (add furosemide, titrate)
  • 3: large/tense or diuretic-resistant: therapeutic paracentesis + albumin
  • 4: recurrent need for paracentesis: TIPS (or liver transplant referral)
  • Fever/abdominal pain: diagnostic tap for SBP first
exam_pearl: TIPS only after repeated paracentesis fails or is needed too often; encephalopathy argues against TIPS.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 60-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Room with increasing ascites. He has no history of fever or decreased level of consciousness. His medications include spironolactone 50 mg/day and furosemide 40 mg/day. His physical examination confirms the presence of large ascites (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This cirrhotic patient has large ascites despite spironolactone and furosemide, with no fever (SBP less likely) and no decreased consciousness (no encephalopathy). Large (tense) or diuretic resistant ascites is treated with therapeutic large volume paracentesis, with IV albumin given when large volumes are removed.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV diuretics have no role in cirrhotic ascites and risk renal impairment and electrolyte disturbance.
C. Raising the oral diuretic dose suits moderate ascites, but it will not relieve large ascites promptly; when diuretics are escalated, spironolactone and furosemide are increased together in a fixed ratio rather than furosemide alone.
D. TIPS is for refractory ascites needing frequent repeated large volume paracentesis, not the next step at this presentation.
key_concept:
Cirrhotic ascites ladder:
  • Treat the cause; sodium restriction
  • Diuretics: spironolactone (drug of choice) with or without furosemide
  • Large/tense or refractory: therapeutic large volume paracentesis + IV albumin
  • Repeated paracentesis needed: TIPS, consider transplant
  • Fever or abdominal pain: diagnostic tap for SBP (neutrophils >250)
exam_pearl: Fever or abdominal tenderness changes the answer to diagnostic paracentesis and IV antibiotics for SBP; its absence here keeps it therapeutic.

stem: Watary diarrhea
key_concept:
Diarrhea pattern decides the organism:
  • Acute vomiting-predominant outbreak: norovirus
  • Chronic watery + bloating + weight loss: Giardia
  • Bloody + fever + seizure in child: Shigella
  • Traveler's watery diarrhea soon after travel: E. coli (ETEC)
  • Rice-water, huge volume: Vibrio cholerae
  • Vomiting a few hours after a meal: S. aureus toxin
exam_pearl: Watery + weight loss + chronic = Giardia; blood and mucus rules out Giardia and norovirus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 40-year-old woman is under treatment for a recurrent helicobacter-associated duodenal ulcer. She noticed that her stool is turned non-tarry black (see lab result). What drug is likely to be the cause of the black stools?
why_right: She is on treatment for recurrent H. pylori ulcer, which means bismuth quadruple therapy. Bismuth reacts with sulfide in the gut to form black bismuth sulfide, giving non-tarry black stool (and sometimes black tongue) with normal hemodynamics and hemoglobin, unlike melena.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ranitidine (H2 blocker) does not discolor stool.
B. Pantoprazole (PPI) does not cause black stool; it is the acid suppressant backbone of eradication regimens.
D. Aluminium hydroxide causes constipation (magnesium antacids cause diarrhea), not black stool.
key_concept:
Black stool: melena or drug?
  • Melena: tarry, sticky, foul, may drop Hb or cause tachycardia
  • Non-tarry black with stable vitals/Hb: bismuth or oral iron
  • Bismuth quadruple: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole (used for recurrence/failure)
  • Aluminium antacid: constipation
exam_pearl: 'Non-tarry' and normal Hb are the clues: harmless bismuth effect, not a rebleed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 32-year-old female on treatment of H.pylori, stool became dark (options Aluminum hydroxide / Bismuth subsalicylate / Ranitidine / PPI); Bismuth subsalicylate highlighted.

stem: patient is diagnosed with celiac disease. Which of the following foods should be avoided?
why_right: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten, and the treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet. Wheat is the main gluten-containing grain, together with barley and rye.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rice is naturally gluten free and is a safe staple in celiac disease.
B. Maize (corn) is gluten free and safe.
C. Potatoes are gluten free and safe.
key_concept:
Gluten-free diet: avoid BRW (Barley, Rye, Wheat).
  • Safe: rice, maize/corn, potatoes
  • Oats: often contaminated with gluten, caution
  • Screen: IgA tTG; confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy)
  • Associations: type 1 DM, dermatitis herpetiformis
exam_pearl: Variant keys barley instead of wheat: any of barley, rye or wheat is the one to avoid.

stem: 35 years old women known case of rheumatic heart disease, she had prosthetic valve replacement 3 years ago, she want to do dental operation. What is the appropriate prophylactic antibiotic?
why_right: A prosthetic valve is a high-risk cardiac condition and a dental operation is a high-risk procedure, so endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated. The standard regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin before the procedure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ampicillin IV/IM is the alternative only when the patient cannot take oral medication; oral amoxicillin is first choice.
C. Clindamycin was the old option for penicillin allergy and is no longer recommended by recent AHA guidance; no allergy is mentioned here.
D. Ceftriaxone IV/IM is a parenteral alternative for patients unable to take oral drugs, not the first-line choice.
key_concept:
IE prophylaxis needs BOTH a high-risk heart AND a high-risk procedure.
  • High-risk heart: prosthetic valve or prosthetic repair material, prior IE, certain congenital heart disease, transplant valvulopathy
  • High-risk procedure: dental work manipulating gingiva/periapical region or perforating mucosa
  • Drug: oral amoxicillin, single dose before
  • Cannot take oral: ampicillin or ceftriaxone IV/IM
  • Not needed: GI/GU procedures, hernia repair, rheumatic disease without prosthesis
exam_pearl: Prosthetic valve but non-dental surgery (e.g. hernia repair) = no IE prophylaxis; prophylaxis is a single pre-procedure dose, not before and after.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient with mechanical valve/rheumatic heart disease undergoing dental procedure. Prophylaxis?' (Erythromycin 300mg or azythro? / Amoxicillin before and after procedure / No treatment); 'Amoxicillin before and after procedure' highlighted.

stem: A 53 yo man post angioplasty after MI 3 monthes ago now complaint on excercise and healthy life style presented to the opd His labs cholesterol was 5.3 and his blood pressure is 139/75 What is the appropriate counseling
highlight_terms_source: post angioplasty after MI 3 monthes ago
why_right: After an MI (here post angioplasty, MI 3 months ago) the patient has established coronary disease, so a lipid lowering drug (high intensity statin) is indicated for secondary prevention regardless of the baseline cholesterol. A total cholesterol of 5.3 mmol/L implies an LDL well above secondary prevention targets, and lifestyle alone will not reach them. That is why the counseling is to start lipid lowering medication on top of his exercise and diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. Annual cholesterol checks are a monitoring step for low risk primary prevention; a post MI patient needs treatment now, not surveillance.
B. Continuing exercise and diet is correct but insufficient on its own; after MI, lifestyle is always combined with statin therapy.
D. BP 139/75 is only borderline (post MI targets are lower, around 130/80), so the first step is lifestyle and repeat readings; an antihypertensive is added if it stays above target, whereas the statin is mandatory after MI.
key_concept:
Established ASCVD (MI, stent, stroke) = statin for life, whatever the cholesterol.
  • Secondary prevention: high intensity statin (e.g. atorvastatin 80) plus lifestyle
  • Primary prevention: risk score decides; lifestyle first if low risk
  • Post MI bundle: antiplatelet, statin, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehab
  • Lifestyle alone is never the answer after an MI
exam_pearl: "Already on diet and exercise" is the distractor: after an MI, the statin is started even if the cholesterol looks only mildly raised.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient with MI 3 month ago. Medically free, on diet and exercise, Bp 136/86, Cholesterol 5.6' (Anti hypertensive / Lipid lowering agent / Continue with exercise and diet); 'Lipid lowering agent' highlighted.

stem: 50 yo male veterinarian complaining of right sacro-iliac pain and fever for 2 monthes. Associated with back pain He also appears agitated, behavioral changes…. It was along long question the labs were HB 10 Low PLT What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: right sacro-iliac pain and fever for 2 monthes
why_right: A veterinarian (animal exposure) with fever for 2 months, sacroiliac and back pain, and behavioral change fits brucellosis: a zoonosis with subacute fever, musculoskeletal involvement (sacroiliitis, spondylitis) and possible neurobrucellosis. Anemia and low platelets reflect marrow and reticuloendothelial involvement, which is typical. The occupational exposure is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. TB can cause chronic fever and spinal disease (Pott's), but it favours the thoracolumbar spine rather than the sacroiliac joint and has no link to animal work; consider it with cough, weight loss or TB contact.
B. Syphilis can cause neuropsychiatric change (neurosyphilis), but not prolonged fever with sacroiliitis; it would fit a sexual history, rash or chancre.
D. Toxoplasmosis (cat or undercooked meat exposure) causes lymphadenopathy or, in immunocompromised patients, brain abscesses; it does not cause sacroiliitis.
key_concept:
Animal contact or raw milk + prolonged fever + back/sacroiliac pain = brucellosis.
  • Organism: Gram negative coccobacillus
  • Features: undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, sacroiliitis, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias
  • Neurobrucellosis: behavioral change, meningitis
  • Initial test: serology (tube agglutination); blood culture confirms
  • Treatment: doxycycline plus rifampicin (or plus an aminoglycoside)
exam_pearl: Sacroiliitis plus fever in a Saudi exam stem points to brucellosis first; TB spine favours the thoracic vertebrae.

stem: Known htn patient presented to the clinic after failed to reach target blood pressure. He is on amlodipine and losartan. His cbc and kidney function are normal. What to add
highlight_terms_source: failed to reach target blood pressure
why_right: He is already on an ARB (losartan) plus a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) and is not at target, with normal kidney function. The standard third step is A + C + D: add a thiazide or thiazide like diuretic (e.g. indapamide). Normal renal function means a thiazide will still work.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ACE inhibitor duplicates the ARB he already takes; combining ACE inhibitor with ARB raises the risk of hyperkalemia and AKI and is avoided.
B. An alpha blocker is a fourth line (resistant hypertension) option, or chosen first when BPH symptoms coexist; it comes after the diuretic.
D. A beta blocker is reserved for a compelling indication (angina, post MI, heart failure, rate control) or later steps; it is not the standard third drug.
key_concept:
Hypertension ladder: A (ACEi or ARB) or C, then A + C, then A + C + D.
  • Step 3 = add thiazide like diuretic (indapamide, chlorthalidone)
  • Step 4 (resistant): spironolactone if K low or normal; else alpha or beta blocker
  • Never combine ACE inhibitor and ARB
  • Severe renal impairment: thiazides lose effect, use a loop diuretic
exam_pearl: Ask what class is missing from A + C + D; if renal function were poor, the diuretic would be a loop instead of a thiazide.

stem: Women came with weakness , ECG (image show Afib), what is the cause of the stroke?
key_concept:
Weakness + AF on ECG = cardioembolic stroke from left atrial thrombus.
  • AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves
  • Flutter: regular sawtooth waves, often regular ventricular rate around 150
  • Stroke risk scored with CHA2DS2-VASc; prior stroke/TIA scores 2
  • Prevention: anticoagulation (DOAC or warfarin), not antiplatelets
exam_pearl: Regular vs irregularly irregular is the single feature that splits flutter from AF on the strip.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient came with SOB and fatigue. He was stable. ECG: showed bradycardia (same pic, Dx not written). Next step in the management?
why_right: The ECG shows bradycardia, and the patient has SOB and fatigue, so the slow rate is causing symptoms. Of the listed options, atropine is the only treatment that raises a slow heart rate; it is the first-line drug in the bradycardia algorithm, with pacing or dopamine/epinephrine next if it fails. Cardioversion and antiplatelets target tachyarrhythmias and ACS, which this is not.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardioversion treats unstable tachyarrhythmias such as VT, SVT or fast AF. It has no role in raising a slow heart rate.
C. Aspirin is for ACS. There is no chest pain or ischemic picture here, and it does nothing for the rate.
D. Dual antiplatelet therapy is for confirmed ACS or after PCI, not for a symptomatic bradyarrhythmia.
key_concept:
Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine first, then pacing or dopamine/epinephrine if atropine fails.
  • Applies to symptomatic HR below 50
  • Unstable signs: hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, acute heart failure
  • First line: IV atropine, repeat up to the maximum dose
  • Atropine fails: transcutaneous/transvenous pacing or dopamine/epinephrine infusion
  • Stable: monitor with atropine and pacer pads ready
  • Then treat the cause (ischemia, electrolytes, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers)
exam_pearl: Atropine is triggered by bradycardia with poor perfusion (hypotension, altered mentation, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure); a truly stable, asymptomatic bradycardia is monitored and its cause treated.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer shown bold in screenshot (screenshot on next page).

stem: A Medically Free Male Was Incidentally Found To Have Atrial Fibrillation (A-Fib) With HR: 110 bpm And BP: 110/70 mmHg. What Is The Best Treatment For Him? (They Didn’t Ask About Rhythm Control)
highlight_terms_source: Incidentally Found To Have Atrial Fibrillation
why_right: This recall's key is aspirin + bisoprolol because the patient has stable AF (BP 110/70) with a fast rate (HR 110) and the stem says rhythm control is not the question, so the core step is rate control with a beta blocker to bring the rate below 100. He is "medically free", so he has no stroke risk factors that would mandate anticoagulation; the source pairs the beta blocker with aspirin as the antithrombotic.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amiodarone is a rhythm control drug (maintaining sinus rhythm); the stem explicitly excludes rhythm control, and it is not first line for rate control in a stable patient without heart failure.
B. Dual antiplatelet therapy is for coronary disease (ACS, stents), not AF; it does nothing for the rate and adds bleeding without adequate stroke protection.
D. A DOAC plus beta blocker is right when the CHA2DS2-VA score is 2 or more (e.g. hypertension, diabetes, age, prior stroke); this patient is medically free, so anticoagulation is not indicated on the score.
key_concept:
Stable AF = rate control first; anticoagulation is decided by CHA2DS2-VA, not by the rhythm.
  • Unstable (hypotension, shock): electrical cardioversion
  • Stable: rate control with beta blocker, non-DHP CCB or digoxin (digoxin if heart failure)
  • Rate target: below 100 bpm
  • Rhythm control (maintain sinus): amiodarone
  • CHA2DS2-VA ≥2: anticoagulate, DOAC first line
  • Warfarin instead of DOAC: mechanical valve, mitral stenosis
exam_pearl: Push CHA2DS2-VA to ≥2 (e.g. prior stroke, or hypertension plus diabetes) and the answer flips to DOAC + beta blocker; a single point only makes anticoagulation a consideration.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed 853 recall (Arabic note: they wrote the diagnosis, very short case, vitals stable, rate probably normal; options amlodipine / aspirin and clopidogrel / aspirin and metoprolol / apixaban and bisoprolol) highlights aspirin and metoprolol (same concept).

stem: Case and he asked, LDL-cholesterol (mmol/L) Optimal range:
why_right: The recall asks for the general "optimal" LDL range, and the source keys <2.5 mmol/L: this corresponds to the classic optimal LDL of below about 100 mg/dL for a person without established atherosclerotic disease. The compiler note adds the fork: without ASCVD aim <2.5, with ASCVD the target is lower (around 2.0 or less).
why_wrong_block:
B. <2.2 mmol/L is not a standard cut off in any major target scheme; it sits between the primary and secondary prevention targets.
C. <2.0 mmol/L is the stricter target used when the patient already has ASCVD (MI, stroke, PAD), per the source's fork; this stem gives no such history.
D. <3.0 mmol/L is the looser goal used only for low risk individuals in risk based schemes, not the optimal value.
key_concept:
LDL targets are risk based: the more established the vascular disease, the lower the target.
  • General optimal / no ASCVD (this recall): <2.5 mmol/L (about 100 mg/dL)
  • Established ASCVD (per source): about 2.0 mmol/L or lower
  • Clinical ASCVD: high intensity statin regardless of baseline LDL
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL: high intensity statin
  • Diabetes aged 40 to 75: at least moderate intensity statin
exam_pearl: If the case mentions MI, stroke or PAD, the expected answer shifts to the lower ASCVD target.
compiler_note: Compiler note: If There Is No ASCVD → <2.5 , If There Is ASCVD → 2.0

stem: Patient with family hx of diabetes 13 to 15 y old with symptoms of thirst and polyuria ivx show Fasting glucose 8 to 10 mmol not sure but above normal range Hb a1c above 7 , 7.8 % options
OptA: Do a random bs to differentiate between pre diabetes and diabetes
why_right: Diabetes is already established in this 13 to 15 year old: classic symptoms (thirst, polyuria) plus two abnormal results, a fasting glucose above 7 and HbA1c 7.8% (≥6.5%), and the strong family history points to youth onset type 2. A metabolically stable adolescent (no ketosis, HbA1c below about 8.5%) is started on lifestyle change plus metformin, the first line drug from age 10.
why_wrong_block: A. No further test is needed to separate prediabetes from diabetes: two different tests are already in the diabetic range, and random glucose is only diagnostic with symptoms when ≥11.1 mmol/L. A confirmatory test is right only when a single abnormal result exists or results are discordant.
key_concept:
Two abnormal results (two different tests, or one test repeated) confirm diabetes; then choose therapy by severity.
  • Diabetes: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥6.5%, 2 h OGTT ≥11.1, random ≥11.1 with symptoms
  • Youth T2DM, stable (no ketosis, HbA1c <8.5%): lifestyle + metformin
  • Youth with ketosis/DKA or HbA1c ≥8.5% with marked symptoms: insulin first, then add metformin
  • Adults, HbA1c 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle + metformin; >10%: insulin
  • Sitagliptin and other DPP-4 inhibitors: add on agents, not first line
exam_pearl: In a young patient with ketosis, DKA or very high glucose, think type 1 (or unstable type 2) and give insulin; with family history, obesity and modest HbA1c, metformin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q restatement: polyuria polydipsia with strong family hx of DM2, HbA1c 7.8, fasting glucose 9; first line medication? 1 Metformin (highlighted) / 2 Sitagliptin.

stem: A young female came for check up or something , BMI 31, HbA1C 7.8 BP normal no other comorbidities What's the first line anti-diabetic?
why_right: An obese young woman (BMI 31) with HbA1c 7.8% and no comorbidities has typical type 2 diabetes. HbA1c between 7.5 and 10% at diagnosis means lifestyle plus metformin, which is first line: weight neutral, no hypoglycemia on its own, and cheap.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) is a second line add on when metformin is not enough or not tolerated.
C. Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonist) helps weight and is preferred as an add on when there is established cardiovascular disease or obesity needing extra weight loss, but it is not the first line starting drug here.
D. Glimepiride (sulfonylurea) causes hypoglycemia and weight gain, a poor choice in an obese patient; it is a later add on.
key_concept:
First line T2DM drug = metformin (with lifestyle) unless contraindicated.
  • HbA1c <7.5% at diagnosis: lifestyle 3 to 6 months first
  • HbA1c 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle + metformin
  • HbA1c >10%: insulin
  • Metformin contraindicated when eGFR <30
  • Sulfonylureas: hypoglycemia, weight gain
  • DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists: add on agents
exam_pearl: Only renal failure (eGFR <30) or HbA1c >10% / ketosis moves you away from metformin as the first drug.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Grouped under 868. Also a screenshot variant ('88- Patient with typical picture of DM2, BMI was high. What is the first line medication for her? A- Sitagliptin B- Liraglutide C- Metformin. Answer: C'), i.e. Metformin.

stem: An adult patient presents with He has a strong family history of diabetes mellitus. Only he hase occasionally thirst and fatigue His fasting blood glucose (FBG ) is 7.5 mmol/L. (No Mention Of A1c) What is the first priority in management?
OptB: Repeat the blood test to distinguish between prediabetes and diabetes
why_right: A single fasting glucose of 7.5 mmol/L with no HbA1c and only vague symptoms (occasional thirst, fatigue) does not yet confirm diabetes. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis needs two abnormal results, so the first priority is to repeat the test (or add HbA1c) before labelling him and starting drugs.
why_wrong_block: A. Metformin is started once diabetes is confirmed (two abnormal results, or a symptomatic random glucose ≥11.1); treating on one unconfirmed fasting value is premature.
key_concept:
One abnormal test = confirm first; two abnormal tests = diagnose and treat.
  • Confirm with a second test on the same visit or repeat the same test on another day
  • Fasting: normal <5.6, prediabetes 5.6 to 6.9, diabetes ≥7.0 mmol/L
  • HbA1c: prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4%, diabetes ≥6.5%
  • Discordant results (one diabetic, one prediabetic): repeat the abnormal one or do OGTT
  • Classic symptoms + random ≥11.1 mmol/L: one test is enough
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a second diabetic value (e.g. HbA1c ≥6.5%) the answer flips to treatment.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, and bloody stools. His mother and siblings have experienced similar symptoms. On physical examination, the abdomen is unremarkable. A fecal occult blood (guaiac) test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 25-year-old with abdominal pain, weight loss and bloody stools, whose mother and siblings had the same picture, fits an autosomal dominant inherited colonic condition: familial adenomatous polyposis. FAP presents in young adults with bleeding, loose stools and weight loss from hundreds of adenomas, and progresses to colorectal cancer if untreated; the unremarkable abdomen fits a mucosal process.
why_wrong_block:
A. Peutz–Jeghers is also autosomal dominant, but it causes hamartomatous small bowel polyps with mucocutaneous lip/buccal pigmentation and often intussusception; no pigmentation is described.
C. Ulcerative colitis gives bloody diarrhea with urgency and mucus; family clustering is weaker and a mother plus siblings all affected points to a dominant polyposis syndrome.
D. Crohn's disease typically causes non bloody diarrhea, RLQ pain or mass, perianal disease and oral ulcers; vertical inheritance in mother and siblings is not its pattern.
key_concept:
Young adult + rectal bleeding + strong vertical family history = FAP.
  • Autosomal dominant, APC gene on chromosome 5q
  • Hundreds to thousands of adenomas ("carpeted with polyps")
  • Cancer is near certain if untreated: prophylactic colectomy
  • Extracolonic: duodenal adenomas, desmoids, osteomas, CHRPE
  • Peutz–Jeghers: hamartomas + mucocutaneous pigmentation
exam_pearl: Freckles on the lips or intussusception flips the answer to Peutz–Jeghers.

stem: A 55-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department complaining of lethargy for the last 2 days. On physical examination, vital signs are stable with unremarkable physical examination. ECG shows no acute changes (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Sodium 139 (134-146 mmol/L); Potassium 6.6 (3.5-5.1 mmol/L); Bicarbonate 15 (21-28 mmol/L); Blood urea nitrogen 9 (2.8 to 8.9 mmol/L); Creatinine 118 (44-115 mol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_right: K 6.6 is significant hyperkalemia, but vitals are stable and the ECG shows no acute changes, so membrane stabilization with calcium is not mandatory. The most appropriate initial treatment is to shift potassium into cells with insulin plus dextrose, which acts within minutes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemodialysis is the last step, used when hyperkalemia is refractory to medical therapy or with severe renal failure or fluid overload; creatinine here is only mildly raised.
B. IV bicarbonate is only an adjunct when there is significant acidosis; despite HCO3 15 it is weaker and slower than insulin/dextrose and is not the initial standard.
D. Normal saline does not meaningfully lower potassium; it is used for volume depletion, which is not present here.
key_concept:
Hyperkalemia ladder: stabilize, shift, remove.
  • ECG changes (peaked T, wide QRS): IV calcium gluconate first
  • Shift: insulin + dextrose, nebulized salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic
  • Remove: binders, loop diuretics
  • Dialysis: refractory cases or renal failure
  • No ECG changes + K 6.6: insulin dextrose
exam_pearl: Peaked T waves on ECG flips the answer to IV calcium gluconate.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version (50 year old male, lethargy, ECG normal, K 6.6, HCO3 15; initial management?) highlights B. Insulin dextrose infusion (options IV NS / Insulin dextrose / IV bicarbonate / Hemodialysis); the fuller Q restatement marks **C. Insulin dextrose infusion. Same answer.

stem: A 55-year-old man is newly diagnosed with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is started on aspirin, metformin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide. A few days later, he develops severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
highlight_terms_source: severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint
why_right: A few days after starting new drugs, he develops acute pain, redness and swelling of the first MTP joint, the classic picture of a gout flare (podagra). Hydrochlorothiazide is the classic drug trigger: thiazides cause hyperuricemia by reducing renal urate excretion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Low dose aspirin can modestly raise urate, but the thiazide is the classic and more likely culprit; aspirin is the answer only if no diuretic is listed.
B. Metformin does not cause hyperuricemia or gout; its key side effects are GI upset, B12 deficiency and lactic acidosis.
C. Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) is not a gout trigger; its classic side effects are dry cough, angioedema and hyperkalemia.
key_concept:
Drugs that precipitate gout raise serum urate.
  • Thiazides and loop diuretics (furosemide): classic triggers
  • Low dose aspirin, cyclosporine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, niacin
  • Losartan lowers urate (useful antihypertensive in gout)
  • Acute flare: NSAID, colchicine or steroids; do not start allopurinol during the attack
exam_pearl: If the drug list has a loop diuretic instead (e.g. furosemide in heart failure), that becomes the culprit.

stem: Patient admit to ICU due to pulmonary embolism , no vital report Which of the following should to give first ?
key_concept:
PE: confirm the diagnosis, then assess circulation.
  • Unstable / massive PE: thrombolysis
  • Unstable + thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy
  • Stable PE: LMWH (enoxaparin)
  • Stable + anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
  • Warfarin and oral agents: long term, not initial for massive PE
exam_pearl: The word "massive" or a low BP in the stem means thrombolysis; a stable patient means enoxaparin.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked (see 880: massive PE, Thrombolysis highlighted).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 35-year-old man, who was medically free, was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with massive pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_right: "Massive pulmonary embolism" in an ICU patient is high-risk (hemodynamically unstable) PE. In a young, "medically free" man there is no contraindication to fibrinolysis, so systemic thrombolysis is the most appropriate initial treatment, followed by heparin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Warfarin is for long-term anticoagulation; it takes days to act and is never initial treatment for acute PE.
C. LMWH is first line for stable PE; massive PE is unstable and needs thrombolysis.
D. Dabigatran is an oral agent for stable or long-term therapy, not for massive PE.
key_concept:
PE treatment depends on circulation.
  • Unstable (massive): thrombolysis, then heparin
  • Thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy
  • Stable: LMWH (or heparin/DOAC), then oral anticoagulation
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE: IVC filter
  • Warfarin: long-term only
exam_pearl: "Massive" or hypotension/shock in a PE stem means thrombolysis; a stable patient gets LMWH.

stem: Patient have recent angin pain and was Dotson with stemi and manage accordingly ،Which of the following will be give for long term
key_concept:
Post MI survival drugs: aspirin, statin (high intensity), beta blocker, ACE inhibitor.
  • Clinical ASCVD: high intensity statin regardless of LDL
  • Aspirin: lifelong low dose; plus a P2Y12 inhibitor after ACS/stent for a defined period
  • Beta blocker: especially with reduced EF
  • ACE inhibitor: reduced EF, diabetes, hypertension
  • CCB and warfarin: no survival benefit in MI
exam_pearl: "High intensity statin" in an option is the usual SMLE target after any MI or stroke.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: What test result is significant or diagnostic for uti
why_right: A urine culture is significant when it grows a single organism at ≥10^5 CFU/mL from a clean catch midstream sample. One uropathogen in high count reflects true bladder infection rather than skin or perineal contamination.
why_wrong_block: A. Mixed bacteria in urine culture: growth of several organisms usually means the sample was contaminated during collection; the right step is to repeat a properly collected sample, not to diagnose UTI.
key_concept:
Significant bacteriuria = one organism at high colony count.
  • Clean catch midstream: ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism
  • Suprapubic aspirate: any growth is significant
  • Catheter sample: lower thresholds are accepted
  • Mixed growth → contamination, repeat sample
  • Positive culture without symptoms = asymptomatic bacteriuria; treat only in pregnancy or before urologic procedures
exam_pearl: A positive culture is not always a UTI to treat: without symptoms in a non-pregnant patient it is asymptomatic bacteriuria.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1571).

stem: A 28-year-old man who was previously healthy, presented to the Emergency Department with 5-days history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, which was associated with nausea and 2 episodes of vomiting. 2 days later, his family noticed yellowish discolouration of his eyes and skin. No history of alcohol or drug use. On examination, he was jaundiced. Abdominal exam showed tender right upper abdomen (see lab results), Test Result Normal Values Alkaline phosphatase 109 39-117 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 990 5-40 IU/L Aspartate aminotransferase 789 12-40 IU/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
why_right: A "previously healthy" 28-year-old with a few days of RUQ pain and vomiting followed by jaundice, with ALT 990 and AST 789 but a normal ALP, has an acute hepatocellular (not cholestatic) hepatitis. In a young person with no alcohol or drug exposure, hepatitis A is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis, and acute infection is confirmed by anti-HAV IgM, which is the most appropriate next diagnostic test.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hepatitis A IgG marks past infection or vaccination (immunity); it stays positive for life and cannot tell you the current illness is hepatitis A.
C. HBsAg is part of a full acute hepatitis screen, but hepatitis B has a long incubation (weeks to months) and less often presents this way; it would be the lead test with risk factors such as unprotected sex, IV drug use or an HBV-positive contact.
D. Hepatitis C rarely causes a symptomatic icteric acute hepatitis and anti-HCV may be negative early; it is tested when there are parenteral risk factors or chronic liver disease.
key_concept:
Acute hepatitis picture (transaminases in the hundreds to thousands, ALP near normal) in a young healthy patient: order HAV IgM.
  • HAV IgM = acute infection; HAV IgG = recovery or immunity
  • HAV: short incubation, faecal oral, self limiting
  • HBV and HCV: incubation weeks to months
  • High ALP with jaundice = cholestatic picture, start with ultrasound instead
exam_pearl: IgM means now, IgG means before; picking HAV IgG is the classic trap.

stem: 46 years old female right handed, complaining of Sausage digits in the left hand and nail pitting, what else you can find in the history?
why_right: "Sausage digits" (dactylitis) plus "nail pitting" is the signature of psoriatic arthritis. The most expected additional history is therefore a dermatological problem, namely psoriatic skin plaques (in the patient or a first degree relative), which usually precede the arthritis.
why_wrong_block: B. Heat intolerance points to hyperthyroidism; thyroid acropachy can cause finger clubbing and swelling, but it does not produce nail pitting with dactylitis.
key_concept:
Dactylitis + nail pitting = psoriatic arthritis; ask about skin psoriasis.
  • Pattern: asymmetric oligoarthritis, DIP involvement, or symmetric polyarthritis
  • Dactylitis, enthesitis (heel pain), sacroiliitis or spondylitis
  • Nails: pitting, onycholysis
  • X-ray: pencil in cup deformity
  • Treatment: NSAID for mild disease, DMARDs for severe
  • Other versions list SLE, RA, pulmonary oedema: RA spares DIPs and lacks nail pitting
exam_pearl: DIP disease with nail changes is psoriatic arthritis, not RA (RA spares the DIPs).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q restatement: young female with DIP joint and knee pain, sausage-shaped fingers; which is expected? A. Dermatologic Problem B. Pulmonary Edema C. SLE D. RA. Answer: A. Dermatologic Problem (psoriatic arthritis).

stem: 44 YO female presented with history of neck swelling for 3 months. She is asymptomatic. Examination revealed thyroid nodule 2x2 cm. What is the best next step?
why_right: In a patient with a palpable thyroid nodule (here 2x2 cm, asymptomatic), the first step of the workup is to check TSH, because thyroid function decides the pathway. A low TSH suggests a hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule that needs a radionuclide scan and rarely needs FNA; a normal or high TSH leads to ultrasound to decide whether FNA is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neck ultrasound is done for essentially every nodule and is ordered alongside TSH, but the algorithm branches on TSH first; ultrasound would be the answer if TSH were already known to be normal.
B. FNA is the diagnostic step for a nodule that meets ultrasound criteria (for example ≥1 to 1.5 cm with suspicious features) and normal or high TSH; it is premature before TSH, and hot nodules usually do not need it.
C. Core needle biopsy is not the standard first tissue test for thyroid nodules; it is reserved for selected cases such as nondiagnostic or indeterminate FNA.
key_concept:
Thyroid nodule: TSH first, then ultrasound, then FNA if criteria met.
  • Low TSH: radionuclide scan (+ US); hot nodule = treat hyperthyroidism, no FNA
  • Cold nodule: back to the US/FNA pathway
  • Normal or high TSH: US to assess FNA criteria
  • Suspicious US features (microcalcifications, hypoechoic) favour FNA
  • Nondiagnostic FNA: repeat FNA
exam_pearl: If the stem already gives a normal TSH or an ultrasound description, the answer moves to FNA.

stem: 67 yo k/c of Afib, htn and depression came with insomnia , irritability and palpitation. On medications amiodarone fluxtion and enalapril.?
why_right: A 67-year-old with AF on amiodarone now has insomnia, irritability and palpitations, which are hyperthyroid symptoms. Amiodarone is iodine rich and can cause either hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, so the first step is to measure thyroxine (free T4) and TSH before attributing the symptoms to depression or treating them blindly.
why_wrong_block:
B. Psychiatric referral assumes the symptoms come from his depression and misses a reversible drug induced thyroid cause; it would be considered only after thyroid function is normal.
C. Propranolol treats the adrenergic symptoms but not the cause and is not the first step; it would be added once thyrotoxicosis is confirmed or for poorly controlled ventricular rate.
key_concept:
New symptoms on amiodarone: check thyroid function (and LFTs) before anything else.
  • Amiodarone toxicity: thyroid (hypo or hyper), lung fibrosis, liver injury, corneal deposits, photosensitivity, blue grey skin
  • Hyperthyroid symptoms: insomnia, irritability, palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance
  • AF can be both a cause and a feature of thyrotoxicosis
exam_pearl: Drug list with amiodarone + psychiatric sounding symptoms = thyroid function test, not psychiatry.

stem: 17 year old complaining of sudden movement stop without falling for 15 seconds while Lip smacking, EEG : 3 Hz spike, what is the management ?
highlight_terms_source: sudden movement stop without falling for 15 seconds
why_right: Brief episodes where activity "stops without falling" for about 15 seconds, with automatisms such as lip smacking, and an EEG showing 3 Hz spike and wave are typical absence seizures. Ethosuximide is a first line drug for absence seizures (valproate is the alternative).
why_wrong_block: B. Phenytoin is used for focal and generalized tonic clonic seizures and status epilepticus; it is ineffective for absence seizures and can worsen them.
key_concept:
Absence seizure: seconds long staring with no postictal state, 3 Hz spike and wave, treat with ethosuximide or valproate.
  • Can be provoked by hyperventilation
  • Automatisms (lip smacking, blinking) can occur in absence
  • Absence with GTC seizures (e.g. juvenile absence in adolescents): valproate covers both
  • Avoid carbamazepine and phenytoin: may aggravate absence
  • Focal impaired awareness seizure: longer, aura, postictal confusion, focal EEG
exam_pearl: 3 Hz spike and wave decides it; lip smacking alone may tempt you toward a focal (temporal) seizure.

stem: 31-year-old woman is evaluated because of daily wheezing and breathlessness that limit her activities several times a week. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. She has never smoked. She is diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. In addition to a short-acting B2-agonist, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
OptA: Add a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting B2-agonist
why_right: "Daily wheezing" that limits activity several times a week defines moderate persistent asthma, which is above the level controlled by ICS alone. The preferred controller at this step is a low dose ICS combined with a LABA (for example budesonide/formoterol), added to the reliever.
why_wrong_block:
B. Low dose ICS alone is the preferred controller for mild persistent asthma (symptoms more than twice weekly but not daily); daily symptoms need the ICS plus LABA step.
C. A leukotriene antagonist is an alternative or add on controller (useful with allergic rhinitis or aspirin sensitive asthma), not the preferred treatment at this step.
D. Theophylline is a less preferred add on because of its narrow therapeutic index, drug interactions and toxicity.
key_concept:
Match severity to step: intermittent SABA; mild persistent low dose ICS; moderate persistent low dose ICS + LABA; severe medium to high dose ICS + LABA.
  • Intermittent: symptoms ≤2 days/week, night waking ≤2/month
  • Mild persistent: >2 days/week but not daily
  • Moderate persistent: daily symptoms, some activity limitation
  • Severe: symptoms throughout the day, extreme limitation
  • LABA is never used without ICS
exam_pearl: "Daily" symptoms means moderate persistent: ICS + LABA, not ICS alone.

stem: 44-year-old man complains of dyspnea on exertion. Heart auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the base of the heart. The intensity and duration of the murmur increase during INSPIRATION. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: The murmur is early diastolic and heard at the base, which narrows it to a semilunar valve regurgitation (aortic or pulmonary). The decisive clue is that its intensity and duration increase during inspiration: inspiration raises venous return to the right heart, so right sided murmurs get louder (the same principle as Carvallo sign in TR). A right sided early diastolic murmur at the base is pulmonary regurgitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mitral regurgitation is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, not a diastolic murmur at the base.
B. Aortic regurgitation is also an early diastolic murmur at the base, but it is left sided and gets softer with inspiration; it is best heard leaning forward in full expiration.
C. Tricuspid regurgitation does increase with inspiration, but it is a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, not early diastolic at the base.
key_concept:
Murmur ID: first systolic vs diastolic, then site, then respiratory variation.
  • Early diastolic at base + louder on inspiration → pulmonary regurgitation
  • Early diastolic at base + louder in expiration, leaning forward → aortic regurgitation
  • Pansystolic at apex → axilla → mitral regurgitation
  • Pansystolic at left lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration → tricuspid regurgitation
  • PR from pulmonary hypertension = Graham Steell murmur
exam_pearl: Same timing and site for AR and PR: inspiration louder = right sided (PR), expiration louder = left sided (AR).

stem: Patient came with early diastolic murmur heard at sternal area and increased by leaning forward. ECG finding: left ventricular hypertrophy. Most likely diagnosis?
why_right: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border that is louder leaning forward (in full expiration) is aortic regurgitation. Chronic volume overload of the left ventricle explains the LVH on ECG. It is the only diastolic lesion among the options that fits this timing and manoeuvre.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mitral stenosis is also diastolic but is a mid diastolic, low pitched rumble with an opening snap, best heard at the apex in the left lateral position; it causes LA enlargement, not LVH.
B. Mitral regurgitation is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
C. Aortic stenosis gives LVH too, but its murmur is ejection systolic at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids.
key_concept:
First classify the murmur as systolic or diastolic, then use site and manoeuvre.
  • Early diastolic, LSE, sitting forward in expiration: AR
  • Mid diastolic rumble at apex, left lateral, opening snap: MS
  • Ejection systolic, aortic area, to carotids: AS
  • Pansystolic, apex, to axilla: MR
  • AR signs: wide pulse pressure, collapsing (Corrigan) pulse, displaced apex
  • Early diastolic murmur louder with inspiration: pulmonary regurgitation
exam_pearl: Diastolic + leaning forward = AR; diastolic + left lateral at apex = MS.

stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of recurrent painful attacks affecting the right big toe, was diagnosed with gout and started on allopurinol. He is also a known case of psoriasis for several years. He presented to the clinic with recurrent joint pain affecting the right big toe, left ankle, and bilateral knees. He is using allopurinol regularly as prescribed but has no improvement in his joint pain. Examinations revealed he has active arthritis at the left ankle and knee joints bilaterally (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause for his joint pain?
why_right: Gout explains the big toe, but it does not explain new active arthritis of the left ankle and both knees that persists despite regular allopurinol. In a man with psoriasis for several years, an asymmetric oligoarthritis of large joints is psoriatic arthritis until proven otherwise. The psoriasis history is the decisive clue the stem plants for you.
why_wrong_block:
A. Active pseudogout arthritis: CPPD typically hits a large joint such as the knee in an older patient (often with OA or hyperparathyroidism); it does not tie in the psoriasis or explain the pattern in a 40-year-old.
B. Active gout arthritis: gout can spread to ankles and knees, but persistent arthritis despite regular allopurinol in a man with long-standing psoriasis points to a second diagnosis. Right when there is no psoriasis and crystals or a high urate explain the flares.
D. Osteoarthritis: degenerative, non-inflammatory disease of older patients; it does not cause active synovitis in a 40-year-old. Right when there is mechanical pain worse with use, osteophytes and joint space narrowing.
key_concept:
Known gout + new arthritis that allopurinol does not settle: look for a second diagnosis in the history.
  • Psoriasis + asymmetric oligoarthritis = psoriatic arthritis
  • Gout: first MTP (podagra), needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals
  • Pseudogout: knee, rhomboid weakly positively birefringent CPPD crystals, chondrocalcinosis
  • OA: older age, worse with activity, non-inflammatory fluid
exam_pearl: A background skin disease in an arthritis stem (psoriasis) is rarely decoration: it usually is the diagnosis.

stem: An elderly who is asymptomatic. ECG: LVH. Echo: Severe bicuspid aortic stenosis. Normal left ventricular ejection fraction. What is the next appropriate management?
why_right: Even though the stenosis is severe (bicuspid valve, LVH on ECG), the patient is asymptomatic with a normal LV ejection fraction. Symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnoea) or LV systolic dysfunction are what trigger valve replacement, so the correct management now is surveillance with serial echocardiography and prompt intervention once symptoms or LV decline appear.
why_wrong_block:
B. TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement, not repair) is indicated for symptomatic severe AS or reduced EF, particularly in elderly or high surgical risk patients; it is not the default in an asymptomatic patient with normal EF.
C. Surgical (mechanical) valve replacement is chosen for symptomatic or LV dysfunction cases, usually younger patients who can take lifelong anticoagulation; it is premature here.
key_concept:
Valve disease rule: asymptomatic = follow up; symptomatic or LV dysfunction = replace.
  • AS triad: angina, syncope, exertional dyspnoea; symptoms predict poor prognosis
  • Asymptomatic severe AS: echo surveillance (commonly every 6 to 12 months)
  • Severe AS with EF <50% or a positive exercise test: intervene
  • Bicuspid valve: AS at a younger age, check for aortic dilation
  • Elderly or high risk: TAVR; younger: surgical AVR
exam_pearl: The single factor that decides surgery timing in AS is symptoms; severity alone does not.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other versions in the block: (1) '70 year old has no sx but k/c of severe aortic stenosis, did ECHO and showed Severe aortic stenosis, LVH, and Normal left ventricle (Forgot the stem)' A- TAVR, B- follow up with echo (highlighted). (2) Screenshot: 'Elderly w aortic stenosis. Asymptomatic. investigation (I think echo): severe stenosis. What to do?' - TAVR, - valvular replacement/mechanical valve (no answer marked). (3) 'Managment of severe asymptomatic Bicuspid aortic stenosis' A. Observe.

stem: Patient has been diagnosed with high cholesterol level and has known history of hypertension and diabetes melitus 2. Lately he feels cramps in muscle and uncomfortable feeling in legs. Which of these medicines is most probably responsible for this?
why_right: A patient recently diagnosed with high cholesterol (so most likely just started on a statin) who now has muscle cramps and leg discomfort has statin associated muscle symptoms. Atorvastatin is the most likely cause; the next step is to check CK and review the dose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Metformin mainly causes GI upset, B12 deficiency and rarely lactic acidosis, not myalgia.
B. Lisinopril causes dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment, not muscle aches.
D. Fibrates are mainly used for high triglycerides; for high cholesterol in a diabetic with hypertension the first line drug is a statin, and fibrate myopathy is mostly a risk when a fibrate is combined with a statin.
key_concept:
Muscle pain on a lipid lowering drug: think statin myopathy; check CK.
  • Myalgia with normal CK to rhabdomyolysis with very high CK
  • Risk rises with high dose, statin + fibrate (especially gemfibrozil), hypothyroidism, CKD
  • Thiazides cause cramps through hypokalaemia; check K
  • ACEI: cough, angioedema, hyperkalaemia
exam_pearl: Cramps with low potassium points to the thiazide; cramps with normal electrolytes after starting cholesterol therapy points to the statin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another version: '60-year-old patient is on lisinopril, thiazide diuretic, and atorvastatin. He presents with muscle weakness and generalized muscle aches. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of his symptoms?' A) Lisinopril B) Thiazide diuretic C) Atorvastatin (highlighted).

stem: A patient on Beta Blocker, ACEI, Salbutamol, and a thiazide diuretic presents with dizziness and muscle cramps. Labs show low potassium. What is the cause of his hypokalemia?
why_right: The question asks for the cause of low potassium in a patient with dizziness and cramps on a regular regimen. Thiazide diuretics increase sodium delivery to the distal nephron and cause renal potassium wasting with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, making the thiazide the most likely chronic cause in this list.
why_wrong_block:
A. Beta blockers blunt beta-2 driven potassium uptake into cells, so they tend to raise serum potassium slightly, not lower it.
B. Salbutamol lowers potassium by shifting it into cells, but the effect is transient and dose related; it becomes the answer in an acute setting with repeated nebulisers, not a stable outpatient regimen with a thiazide.
D. ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and cause hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.
key_concept:
Drugs and potassium: thiazide and loop diuretics, beta-2 agonists and insulin lower K; ACEI/ARB, spironolactone and beta blockers raise K.
  • Thiazide: low K, low Na, high Ca, high uric acid, high glucose, metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypokalaemia features: weakness, cramps, ileus, arrhythmia, flat T and U waves
  • Beta-2 agonist: intracellular shift, short lived
  • Insulin: intracellular shift (DKA treatment)
exam_pearl: Acute nebulised salbutamol with a sudden potassium drop is salbutamol; a chronic regimen with a thiazide is the thiazide.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under the 928 block (Q:), with printed 'Answer: C'.

stem: Pt went to africa, came back with intermittent fever & “malaria symptoms” , whats appropriate tx:
why_right: A traveller back from Africa with intermittent fever and a malaria picture has malaria until a smear proves otherwise. This recall's key is Chloroquine because, per the recaller, it was the only antimalarial offered; every other option was an antibacterial or antiviral that does nothing against Plasmodium. Treat it as an elimination question: pick the one drug that actually acts on the parasite.
why_wrong_block: A. Vancomycin (and the other listed drugs): antibacterials or antivirals with no antimalarial activity. Vancomycin is right for MRSA or other resistant Gram positive infection, or oral therapy for C. difficile.
key_concept:
Febrile traveller from Africa = malaria first; confirm with blood smears and treat by species, severity and region.
  • Diagnosis: thick and thin smears, repeated if the first is negative
  • Africa: mostly P. falciparum, widely chloroquine resistant
  • Uncomplicated falciparum: artemisinin based combination therapy (ACT)
  • Severe malaria: IV artesunate
  • Chloroquine: only for chloroquine sensitive species or regions (e.g. many P. vivax areas)
  • Prophylaxis for endemic travel: atovaquone/proguanil (alternatives doxycycline, mefloquine)
exam_pearl: If ACT or artesunate is among the options for falciparum from Africa, it beats chloroquine; chloroquine wins only when it is the sole antimalarial listed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot of related recall: 'child went to africa what prophylaxis u should give -> Chloroquine'. Note: At this point we need to know the specific region he traveled to along with other options (eg Atovaquone/Proguanil OR Doxycycline OR Mefloquine). Recaller said the other options were antibiotics or antiviral, not for malaria, so 'Then Chloroquine It Is'.

stem: Pt presented with st depression and elevated troponin (no time given) Whats the BEST tx to INITIATE?
why_right: ST depression with elevated troponin is NSTEMI (troponin separates it from unstable angina; no ST elevation separates it from STEMI). The lead-in asks what to initiate: every NSTE-ACS patient starts dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) plus an anticoagulant such as heparin, while the timing of angiography is then decided by risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. Primary angioplasty: the emergency reperfusion strategy for STEMI. In NSTEMI, angiography is an early invasive step timed by risk (immediate only if very high risk, e.g. shock, refractory pain, dangerous arrhythmia), not the first therapy started.
C. Aspirin, clopidogrel and thrombolytic: thrombolysis gives no benefit and adds bleeding risk in NSTEMI or unstable angina; it is used only in STEMI when primary PCI is not available in time.
key_concept:
ECG decides reperfusion; troponin decides UA vs NSTEMI.
  • STEMI: ST elevation or new LBBB, reperfuse now (primary PCI, thrombolysis if PCI unavailable)
  • NSTEMI: ST depression/T inversion + raised troponin
  • Unstable angina: same ECG, normal troponin
  • NSTE-ACS start: aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor + anticoagulant (heparin/LMWH)
  • Add: beta blocker, high intensity statin, nitrate for pain
exam_pearl: Thrombolytics never belong in NSTEMI or unstable angina: any option pairing them with ST depression is a trap.

stem: A pt k/c hypertension diabetes presents with increased sob , hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea Echo shows LV hyper atrophy Labs shows 500 bnb - normal 300 1 Troponin - normal 0.07 What is the type of shock?
why_right: Hypertension and diabetes with LV hypertrophy on echo, a raised BNP and a clearly raised troponin (1 vs normal 0.07) point to a failing myocardium. Add shortness of breath, hypotension and tachycardia and this is pump failure with low output: cardiogenic shock. Nothing in the stem suggests blood loss, spinal injury or an extracardiac obstruction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemorrhagic: needs a source of bleeding (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured aneurysm) and would not raise BNP or troponin with LV disease on echo; the problem there is volume loss, not pump failure.
B. Neurogenic: follows spinal cord injury and gives hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin; this patient is tachycardic with no neurological trigger.
C. Obstructive: tamponade, massive PE or tension pneumothorax; echo would show an effusion or a dilated strained right ventricle, not LV hypertrophy, and there is no sudden trigger.
key_concept:
Classify shock by volume problem vs output problem.
  • Cardiogenic: pump failure, high PCWP, pulmonary congestion, raised BNP
  • Obstructive: tamponade (Beck triad), massive PE, tension pneumothorax
  • Hypovolemic/hemorrhagic: low filling pressures, cold peripheries
  • Septic: warm peripheries, high cardiac output, low SVR
  • Neurogenic: spinal injury, hypotension + bradycardia
exam_pearl: Hypotension with dyspnea, raised BNP and a diseased LV on echo points to the pump (cardiogenic); obstructive shock needs an effusion, a strained RV or a tension pneumothorax.

stem: Seizure and jerky movement arm involvement (for a short time; what type of seizure? these were the only options recalled)
why_right: Jerky movement of the arm lasting only a short time describes myoclonic seizures: sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks, often of the arms, usually with preserved awareness. The brevity is the decisive clue; a clonic seizure is a sustained run of rhythmic jerking.
why_wrong_block: B. Clonic: repetitive, rhythmic jerking that continues over a longer period, usually with impaired consciousness. Right when the stem describes sustained rhythmic jerks rather than a single brief jerk.
key_concept:
Name the seizure by what the body does and for how long.
  • Myoclonic: brief shock-like jerks, often arms, awareness kept (e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, morning jerks)
  • Clonic: sustained rhythmic jerking
  • Tonic: sustained stiffening
  • Atonic: sudden loss of tone, drop attack
  • Absence: brief staring spell, unresponsive, no postictal state
exam_pearl: "Brief jerk" = myoclonic; "rhythmic jerking that goes on" = clonic.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Arabic note translated: it was for a short time; what type of seizure; the options were only these ones I remember.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented with shortness of breath, fatigue, and nighttime cough. He has been working in a car repair shop for the past 1 year and notes that his symptoms began about 8 months ago. He believes his symptoms are associated with his workdays. He is being evaluated after several days off from work and currently has no symptoms or medical concerns. He has an unremarkable medical history and takes no medications. He has never smoked. Physical examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph and spirometry results are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: symptoms are associated with his workdays
why_right: Symptoms linked to "workdays" in a car repair worker (paint and isocyanate exposure) raise occupational asthma. He is being tested "after several days off", so normal spirometry does not exclude it. The next step is to objectively confirm the work link by repeating spirometry (or serial peak flows) after workplace exposure before treating or changing jobs.
why_wrong_block:
A. High-resolution CT is for suspected interstitial lung disease or bronchiectasis; it cannot diagnose occupational asthma and the chest X-ray is normal.
B. Starting a daily inhaled glucocorticoid before confirming the diagnosis is premature; treatment comes after objective confirmation.
C. Advising a job change is a major step that needs a confirmed diagnosis first; it becomes right once occupational asthma is proven.
key_concept:
Suspected occupational asthma with normal tests away from work: retest after exposure.
  • Clue: symptoms worse on workdays, better on days off or holidays
  • Car repair and spray painting: isocyanates; bakers: flour
  • Confirm with spirometry or serial peak flow at and away from work
  • Methacholine challenge if spirometry stays normal but suspicion is high
  • Definitive management: remove from the exposure
exam_pearl: Normal spirometry done on days off does not rule out occupational asthma; test after exposure.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 3 years is evaluated in the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of pain and swelling of the left knee and low-grade fever. There was no history of trauma. Her medications are prednisone, methotrexate, and etanercept. Joints examination reveals a swollen and tender left knee, and mild synovitis is present on the third proximal interphalangeal joint bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
OptC: Conventional radiology of the left knee
OptD: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left knee
highlight_terms_source: pain and swelling of the left knee and low-grade fever
why_right: A single, acutely swollen, tender knee with low-grade fever in an RA patient who is immunosuppressed (prednisone, methotrexate, etanercept) is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Arthrocentesis with Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals is the initial step, together with blood cultures, before antibiotics. The mild PIP synovitis is just her background RA.
why_wrong_block:
A. A bone scan is non-specific and slow; it cannot distinguish infection from inflammation and delays aspiration of a possibly septic joint.
C. Plain X-ray may be done as a baseline, but it is usually normal early in septic arthritis and does not exclude infection.
D. MRI is useful for osteomyelitis or internal derangement but does not replace joint fluid analysis in an acute monoarthritis.
key_concept:
Acute monoarthritis: tap the joint first.
  • Septic arthritis must be excluded in every acute monoarthritis
  • Risk: RA, joint damage, immunosuppression (steroids, anti-TNF)
  • Synovial WBC very high, neutrophil predominant, Gram stain/culture
  • Crystals: gout (negatively birefringent needles), pseudogout (positively birefringent rhomboids)
  • Anti-TNF and steroids can blunt fever
exam_pearl: One joint flaring out of proportion to the rest in RA = septic arthritis, not an RA flare.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0283).

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of fever, night sweats, fatigue, arthralgia, and lower back pain. He had a history of unpasteurized milk ingestion. His examination reveals right knee arthritis and limited spinal movements. His cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable (see lab results and reports). Right knee joint aspiration: WBC 15,000 (0-200). Blood culture: Negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?
why_right: "Unpasteurized milk" plus a "4-month" undulating fever, night sweats, arthralgia, "lower back pain" with "limited spinal movements" and knee arthritis is osteoarticular (chronic) brucellosis. Blood cultures are frequently negative in chronic disease, so the practical next step is Brucella serology (standard tube agglutination test).
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver biopsy: invasive and not needed; it would be considered for granulomatous hepatitis of unclear cause, not when a simple serologic test can confirm the diagnosis.
B. Bone marrow biopsy/culture: has a higher yield than blood culture for Brucella, but it is invasive and kept for when serology is equivocal; it is not the first move.
C. Repeat blood culture: blood cultures are often negative in chronic brucellosis and are slow (fastidious organism), so repeating them delays diagnosis; serology is the answer here.
key_concept:
Brucellosis = raw milk + undulant fever + osteoarticular disease (sacroiliitis, spondylitis, large joint arthritis).
  • Organism: Gram negative coccobacillus
  • First test: serology (tube agglutination)
  • Blood culture: often negative in chronic cases; marrow culture has higher yield
  • Treatment: doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin
  • Spondylitis/osteoarticular disease: longer course (about 3 months)
exam_pearl: Raw milk + back pain + negative blood culture: do not chase cultures or biopsies; send Brucella serology.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another version later in the block: 'A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of fever, fatigue, and lower back pain. He had a history of unpasteurized milk ingestion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?' C. blood culture, D. Antibody titer (highlighted).
